study.title: Romans 10 - Justice by faith, proclamation of the gospel, and the refusal of Israel
study.overview: Romans 10 counters two ways of seeking acceptance before God: righteousness based on the Law and the righteousness received by faith in Christ. Paul begins with his pain and desire for Israel's salvation, recognizing his religious zeal, but stating that this zeal was without understanding because they sought to establish their own righteousness. He then shows that Christ is the fulfillment of the Law and that the message of salvation is near, accessible by the word of faith: to believe in the heart in the resurrection of Jesus and to confess him as Lord. Finally, Paul explains that salvation reaches Jews and Gentiles without distinction, but also that Israel's unbelief is not due to the lack of divine testimony, for God sent preachers, faith comes by hearing, and the prophets themselves had already announced both the inclusion of the Gentiles and the persistent resistance of Israel.

outline.title: Paul's desire for Israel and the contrast between the Law and faith
outline.explanation: Paul begins by declaring his prayer for the salvation of Israel. He recognizes their zeal for God, but denounces the lack of understanding: by seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not subjected themselves to the righteousness of God. Christ is presented as the end of the Law for the righteousness of every one who believes, that is, the target and the fulfillment to which the Law pointed out.

outline.title: The righteousness of faith is close, simple and universal
outline.explanation: Paul quotes Moses to show that the logic of the Law requires integral obedience, while the logic of faith does not command to ascend to heaven or descend into the abyss to bring Christ, because the word has already been brought near. The appropriate answer is to believe in the heart that God raised Jesus and confess him with his mouth as Lord. This salvation makes no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is rich for all who call upon him.

outline.title: The need for Israel's preaching and responsibility
outline.explanation: Paul chains questions to show that invoking depends on believing, believing depends on hearing, listening depends on the preacher sent. Faith comes by hearing the word of God, and Israel cannot claim a lack of proclamation: the gospel has been widely proclaimed. Even so, many did not obey, as the Scriptures already indicated. The prophets also announced that God would attain to those who did not seek him before, while Israel remained a rebellious and resilient people.

study.context: The chapter dialogues with the tension between Israel and the Gentiles within the history of salvation. The notes highlight that, in Paul's time, the rejection of the Messiah by many Jews was understood in the light of opposition to the righteousness of God revealed in Christ. It is also noteworthy that the inclusion of the Gentiles was already prefigured in the prophecies cited by Paul. The text does not depend on archaeological details or specific dates for its main reading; its focus is theological and biblical.
study.theology: Romans 10 teaches that salvation is not attained by legal merit, but by the righteousness that comes from God through faith in Christ. The Law is good, but it was not given as a way for anyone to produce his own righteousness before God; he points to Christ and finds in him his purpose. The gospel is accessible and close: God does not require an impossible religious escalation, but calls the sinner to believe in the resurrection of Jesus and to confess him as Lord. There is also a strong missionary emphasis: God saves through preaching, and faith is born from hearing the word announced. Finally, the chapter affirms the unity of the divine offering of salvation for Jews and Gentiles, while at the same time that Israel's persistent unbelief holds as conscious resistance to the revelation received.

scholarViews.insight: Paul describes Israel's zeal as real but diverted, because they did not understand that Jesus Christ is the culmination of God's plan and tried to establish their own righteousness rather than submit to the righteousness of God.

The apostle demonstrates that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles as to the way of acceptance before God; the same Lord is that of all and treats both with the same grace in the way of the gospel.
Israel's refusal was not caused by a lack of warning, but by obstinacy: God was willing to receive them, extending their hands, although they remained disobedient and contradicters.

questions: In what areas can I be trying to establish my own righteousness rather than submit to the righteousness of God in Christ?
Is my faith linked to constant listening to the word of God and to the sincere confession of Jesus as Lord?
How does my life share in God's mission, so that others may hear the gospel through me?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a double call: to abandon any confidence in religious performance and to embrace with simplicity the justice received by faith. Then examine if your confession of Jesus as Lord is accompanied by consistent life. Finally, pray for people who still resist the gospel and willing to be, in a practical way, one who brings the word of God to others with clarity, humility and perseverance.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not bring comments verse to verse for all sections, so the synthesis of some excerpts was built directly from the biblical text, in harmony with the points explicitly present in the excerpts. Historical or geographical data beyond what the notes support were also not used. The expression 'end of the Law' was understood here, based on the context and notes, as fulfillment and target of the Law in Christ, without imposing a single denominational formulation.
